author: Miles_Brundage
text:
It's hard to say which classes or specific use cases will spread the most.

But it seems safe to say that the era of almost-exclusively-human-generated and almost-never-individually-customized media will not last much longer, absent consumer/policy demand for it continuing. /Fin

author: Miles_Brundage
text: And people can always choose not to customize their content. But currently we're largely accepting (if not seeking out) mass customization of a different kind, namely customization of *which* content we are exposed to via feeds.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
In some sense, mass transforming of media is less scary than an ecosystem flooded with machine-generated content: at least the content was originally from humans* and we're all *kind* of consuming the same thing. 

*well, maybe. These aren't mutually exclusive categories, again.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Imagine e.g. Netflix taking commands to remove scenes that would scare you specifically, or to substitute you for the protagonist. Or Spotify remixing all of the songs you listen to in the style of your favorite DJ, or reading Kindle books with footnotes written just for you.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: An Internet flooded with machine-generated, novel content threatens a sense of shared truth, whereas routine transformation of media threatens a sense of shared experience.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
Summarization might also be an example of this (transforming the length of text while preserving as much of the meaning as possible). 

But I could see transformation having as big an impact as de novo content generation, or more, since it could enable extreme customization.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Some of this is happening already, and the boundaries are blurry, e.g. you might call auto-generation of captions for a video "transformation" (audio-->text), and depending on whether there's a human in the loop, it might also be thought of as substitution or augmentation.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
What these two use case classes have in common is that they're both about generating *new* content. 

A third class might be called transformation, where the aim is to take existing media and transform it, either within the same modality (e.g. text-->text) or across modalities.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
Autocomplete is an example of augmentation. 

People talk about augmentation a lot, but existing use cases are often about doing an existing X more easily, vs. doing things that weren't at all possible before.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: With augmentation, humans and GMs divide up labor in some way, e.g. GM generates multiple candidates + human selects among them. In practice today, many substitution-sounding use cases are really augmentation, due to edge cases/need for human-in-the-loop in some contexts etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
For stuff like that (let's call them substitution use cases), it's ~straightforward to think about possible upsides/downsides - imagine something getting cheaper and faster.

A second class of use cases sounds very different, but isn't as different as it sounds: augmentation.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
The simplest* use cases to think about are ones where a GM generates media that could otherwise be created by a human, but are faster/cheaper when done by a GM. Examples include voice for Duplex customer service bots or generating text w/ a language model.

*still not that simple

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The growing ability of generative models to create realistic text/audio/images/video has sparked much excitement and concern, and led to valuable work on anticipating/mitigating/preventing related risks. But I think we're still pretty clueless about the key GM use cases (thread).

text: P.S. to clarify, since my first tweet was maybe misleading - "MT could be huge + its impacts are/will be uneven" aren't novel points, which is why there are communities/projects focused on low resource translation. The specific analogies/effects discussed are what's notable here.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Overall, an interesting paper and worth checking out for those interested in MT's social/economic impacts. And it's always nice to see more analysis of AI's effects that is both clear-eyed re: the default likelihood of uneven benefits, while also suggesting concrete improvements.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: I liked the example of Japanese ski manufacturers, who, facing competition from American ski manufacturers via int'l trade, argued that Japanese snow is special and therefore special, longer skis are needed there.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
Last main takeaway I'll mention [this is not comprehensive at all, def. check out the paper if any of this sounds interesting]: 

Reducing the role of language in differentiating some individuals/groups from others could increase the relative importance of other differences.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
(again, he emphasizes the immediate-ish future and a "default" scenario where translation proceeds very evenly but he has interesting ideas for incentivizing a better path) 

Another point in the paper: MT could make possible larger scale political movements, for good and/or ill.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: He also makes a nice analogy to the early stages of MRIs, where abundant new info (vs. X-rays) produced false positives, i.e. diagnosing problems that weren't there. Similarly, "false positives" in cross-lingual understanding via seemingly good translation could cause conflict

author: Miles_Brundage
text: "Railroads vastly reduced the impact of physical distance between particular nodes in a network and, in relative terms at least, increased the barriers between others." Likewise, MT might by default entrench the dominance of certain clusters of language/ideas/culture/economies.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Given these assumptions, he sketches some possible implications for social and economic change. For example, in terms of trade in both goods and ideas, the railroad analogy is ominous -

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Weber focuses on the 2020s, i.e. when MT is likely to improve but remain imperfect, and on the "default" scenario of high-resource languages/language dyads advancing more than low-resource languages/language dyads - though he suggests some policies to help address that imbalance.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @catherineols Others may have different senses of these terms, ofc, and one could define advanced similarly to how I defined powerful. But in practice I am often very unclear what people mean when they say "advanced" FWIW.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @catherineols In my head "powerful" = ~"can do lots of stuff" which seems to track what people are often interested in (and it's often true), whereas "advanced" is not obviously related to capabilities (vs. fancy underlying techniques). So, not *much* more precise but at least often accurate.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: People often mean something like "powerful," "state of the art," "impressive," etc., so they should just use those terms instead (I'm saying this to myself as much as to others, because I've used "advanced" before).

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
Ban the word "advanced" in the context of software/AI - e.g. "advanced artificial intelligence," "advanced algorithms." 

It adds nothing substantive, often refers to standard/old (non-advanced?) techniques, and just makes the tech sound harder to understand than it is.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: So where does the report leave us? As the title suggests (“Toward” ... ”supporting”), there’s no quick overnight fix for these issues. We didn’t cover everything being done or think of everything that could be done to make progress here, though we hope the report is a good step.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: We organize them into “institutional,” “software,” and “hardware” mechanisms, though these are fuzzy lines and we note various interconnections between them. For example, third party auditing of AI systems is an institutional mechanism, but relies on/involves software + hardware.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: These are ways of providing or assessing evidence about the properties of AI systems. Many exist + could exist - we survey and try to extend the toolbox. Specifically, we analyze mechanisms that help verify claims about AI systems being safe, secure, fair, or privacy-preserving.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: There’s been great work articulating ethical principles to guide AI development, and regulators are starting to specify concrete standards for the properties of AI systems. But how can you verify when those principles are applied? That’s where what we call “mechanisms” come in.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: So who cares about “verifiable claims”? Lots of people should and already do! We argue that a lot of (not all) issues related to trust + AI involve the need for effective external scrutiny of claims made about AI systems + development processes.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Super excited to share a report I’ve been working on with a bunch of colleagues from different orgs since last year. Building on a workshop last April, we analyze various ways to improve the verifiability of claims about AI systems. You can read it here: https://t.co/nkyM4rxQJg

Extremely excited + proud to share a new report that is by far the largest academic project I’ve been honored to be a part of: “Toward Trustworthy AI Development: Mechanisms for Supporting Verifiable Claims” @ https://t.co/fvingGsemN
Parallel to my recent work with @roeldobbe , excited to share a piece I co-wrote on the need for verification mechanisms to address large-scale AI impacts: https://t.co/OI4OaEKaBs

author: Miles_Brundage
text: On the malicious end, consider e.g. “real-time” fine-tuning on different targets in the context of a disinformation campaign or spear phishing campaign. Suspect this isn’t the low hanging fruit for malicious uses of LMs RN but worth considering how things could evolve over time.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Already, there is large-scale application of FTish stuff, e.g. Google’s Smart Reply involves explicitly mixing outputs from a base model + a custom model trained on your recent sent messages. But I suspect other applications are possible, some desirable + some harmful.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 5. Expertise is still needed to FT “optimally” (i.e. get SOTA, though we don’t really know what optimal FT means/entails). However, the ease of getting decent results and the speed with which it happens make it amenable to non-experts - and potentially automation.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 4. More on the democratization theme: it’s not just that FT lowers the barrier to entry, but that it brings it into the realm of *easy and fast for non-experts.* It’s wild that one can e.g. FT in minutes on a custom dataset using freely available computing power (e.g. Colab).

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
3. FT raises lots of issues around responsibility, as it complicates the AI model “supply chain.” See e.g. this paper from @lrvarshney et al. on some aspects of this: https://t.co/wvrt1zYSuK

How to document models for biases in an FT context is an esp. interesting question IMO.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: FT generally is “democratizing” AI (though I don’t like that term) for many, but moreso among speakers of high-resource languages + people w/ applications that don’t require 100% reliability, and those studying tasks that occur “naturally” in the wild on the Internet.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
For scientific, creative, + commercial purposes, fine-tuning is amazing - super fast and easy compared to starting from scratch for a new task, and the # of LM fine-tuning successes is growing rapidly.
